parameters.name: sample_size
parameters.description:
Spatial extent of the field the model operates on.  For the
paper's ImageNet models this is the VAE latent, `32`, not the
256-pixel image.

parameters.name: in_channels
parameters.description:
Latent channels.  Four is the standard VAE tokenizer's width;
the CIFAR-10 experiment works in pixel space at three.  The
average velocity is a displacement in the sample's own space, so
the two must be equal.

parameters.name: out_channels
parameters.description:
Latent channels.  Four is the standard VAE tokenizer's width;
the CIFAR-10 experiment works in pixel space at three.  The
average velocity is a displacement in the sample's own space, so
the two must be equal.

parameters.name: patch_size
parameters.description:
Side of the square patch each token covers.  The suffix in the
paper's variant names — `B/2` is the Base backbone at patch 2.

parameters.name: hidden_size
parameters.description: Transformer width.

parameters.name: depth
parameters.description: Number of transformer blocks.

parameters.name: num_heads
parameters.description: Attention heads per block.

parameters.name: mlp_ratio
parameters.description: Feed-forward expansion inside each block.

parameters.name: num_classes
parameters.description:
Label vocabulary for class conditioning.  The extra index
`num_classes` is the unconditional token the guidance dropout
substitutes.

parameters.name: class_dropout
parameters.description:
Probability of replacing the label with the unconditional token
during training, which is what leaves the model able to produce
the unconditional field guidance needs.

parameters.name: time_conditioning
parameters.description:
Which time variables the network is conditioned on.  The
Jacobian-vector product is always taken with respect to
$u_\theta(\cdot, r, t)$ regardless of this choice — the
encoding changes the network's inputs, not the identity.

parameters.name: time_sampler
parameters.description: Distribution the pair `(r, t)` is drawn from.

parameters.name: lognorm_mean
parameters.description:
Parameters of the normal that `"lognorm"` squashes through the
logistic.  The paper's ImageNet setting; its CIFAR-10 setting is
`(-2.0, 2.0)`.

parameters.name: lognorm_std
parameters.description:
Parameters of the normal that `"lognorm"` squashes through the
logistic.  The paper's ImageNet setting; its CIFAR-10 setting is
`(-2.0, 2.0)`.

parameters.name: ratio_r_not_t
parameters.description:
Fraction of the batch that gets $r \neq t$.  The rest
trains the instantaneous velocity, which is what anchors the
field.  Zero reduces the method to Flow Matching and does not
produce usable one-step samples.

parameters.name: adaptive_weight_power
parameters.description:
$p$ in the loss weight $w = 1/(\lVert\Delta\rVert^2 + c)^p$.  `0` is the plain squared error; `0.5` is close to the
pseudo-Huber loss of prior one-step work.

parameters.name: adaptive_weight_eps
parameters.description:
$c$ above — keeps the weight finite where the error is
near zero.

parameters.name: guidance_scale
parameters.description:
$\omega$ in the guided target.  One disables guidance and
recovers the plain objective.

parameters.name: guidance_mix
parameters.description:
$\kappa$, which mixes the model's own class-conditional
average velocity into the target alongside the class-unconditional
one.  The effective scale a sampler sees is
$\omega' = \omega / (1 - \kappa)$.

parameters.name: guidance_interval
parameters.description:
The range of $t$ over which guidance is applied at all.
The larger models restrict it; `XL/2+` uses `(0.3, 0.8)`.

examples:
>>> from lucid.models.generative.mean_flow import MeanFlowConfig
>>> config = MeanFlowConfig()
>>> config.hidden_size, config.depth, config.patch_size
(768, 12, 2)
The variant names encode the backbone size and the patch side, so
L/2 is the Large backbone tokenised at two:
>>> large = MeanFlowConfig(hidden_size=1024, depth=24, num_heads=16)
>>> large.num_patches
256
notes:
Reference: Geng, Deng, Bai, Kolter, and He, *"Mean Flows for One-step
Generative Modeling"*, [arXiv:2505.13447](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13447), 2025.  Architecture and
training settings are Table 4; the ablations that pin the defaults
are Table 1.

The backbone is DiT's, unchanged — the paper is explicit that it
keeps "the DiT architecture blocks untouched" and that architectural
improvements are orthogonal.  What differs from a diffusion DiT is
only the conditioning: two time variables rather than one, each
embedded and passed through a two-layer MLP before being summed.

methods.name: __init__
methods.summary: Initialise the model. See the class docstring for parameters.

methods.name: forward
methods.signature: forward(images: Tensor, labels: Tensor | None = None)
methods.summary: One training step of the MeanFlow objective.

parameters.name: images
parameters.description: `(B, C, H, W)` — data, or the VAE latent of it.

parameters.name: labels
parameters.description:
`(B,)` class indices.  Dropped to the unconditional token
with probability `MeanFlowConfig.class_dropout`, which
is what leaves the model able to produce both fields.

returns.description: The weighted loss, the prediction and the target.

notes:
The Jacobian-vector product is taken along $(v, 0, 1)$ —
the tangent that the chain rule gives for
$\frac{d}{dt}u(z_t, r, t)$ once $dz_t/dt = v$ and
$dr/dt = 0$ are substituted.  Any other tangent trains a
different quantity: the paper's destructive ablation reports FID
61.06 for this one and 137–329 for the alternatives.

methods.name: generate
methods.signature: generate(n_samples: int = 1, labels: Tensor | None = None, steps: int = 1, noise: Tensor | None = None, device: str | None = None)
methods.summary: Sample by walking the average velocity backwards from noise.

parameters.name: n_samples
parameters.description: How many to draw.

parameters.name: labels
parameters.description:
`(n_samples,)` class indices.  `None` samples the
unconditional field.

parameters.name: steps
parameters.description:
Network evaluations.  One is the point of the method:
$z_0 = z_1 - u(z_1, 0, 1)$ covers the whole path.  More
subdivide $[0, 1]$ and apply Eq. 12 on each piece, which
the paper notes is straightforward and reports at two.

parameters.name: noise
parameters.description: Starting point $z_1$.  Drawn when absent.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Where to draw.  Defaults to the model's own device.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.mean_flow import (
...     MeanFlowConfig, MeanFlowForImageGeneration)
>>> config = MeanFlowConfig(sample_size=8, patch_size=2,
...                         hidden_size=32, depth=2, num_heads=4,
...                         num_classes=10)
>>> model = MeanFlowForImageGeneration(config).eval()
>>> model.generate(2).samples.shape
(2, 4, 8, 8)

methods.name: __init__
methods.summary: Initialise the network. See the class docstring for parameters.

methods.name: forward
methods.signature: forward(z: Tensor, r: Tensor, t: Tensor, labels: Tensor | None = None)

parameters.name: z
parameters.description: `(B, in_channels, H, W)` — the point on the path.

parameters.name: r
parameters.description: `(B,)` — the interval's start.

parameters.name: t
parameters.description: `(B,)` — the interval's end, and where `z` lives.

parameters.name: labels
parameters.description:
`(B,)` class indices.  `None` uses the unconditional
token, which is index `num_classes`.

returns.description:
`sample` of shape `(B, out_channels, H, W)` —
$u_\theta(z, r, t)$.  `loss` stays `None`: the
objective lives in `MeanFlowForImageGeneration`.

parameters.name: config
parameters.description: The variant to build.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.mean_flow import (
...     MeanFlowConfig, MeanFlowModel)
>>> config = MeanFlowConfig(sample_size=8, patch_size=2, hidden_size=32,
...                         depth=2, num_heads=4, num_classes=10)
>>> model = MeanFlowModel(config).eval()
>>> z = lucid.randn((1, 4, 8, 8))
>>> t = lucid.tensor([1.0])
>>> r = lucid.tensor([0.0])
>>> model(z, r, t).sample.shape
(1, 4, 8, 8)
notes:
Reference: Geng, Deng, Bai, Kolter, and He, *"Mean Flows for One-step
Generative Modeling"*, [arXiv:2505.13447](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13447), 2025.  Backbone
configurations are Table 4.

The forward takes both times.  Which of them reach the embedding is
`MeanFlowConfig.time_conditioning`; the signature does not
change with it, because the Jacobian-vector product the objective
needs is always taken with respect to $(z, r, t)$ no matter how
the network chooses to encode them.

attributes.name: patch_embed
attributes.description:
Patchifying projection — stride equals kernel, so patches do not
overlap.

attributes.name: pos_embed
attributes.description: Frozen two-dimensional sine-cosine table, added to the tokens.

attributes.name: final
attributes.description: Modulated norm and projection back to patch space.

members.name: MeanFlowOutput
members.signature: MeanFlowOutput(loss: Tensor, prediction: Tensor, target: Tensor)

methods.name: __init__
methods.summary: Initialise the head. See the class docstring for parameters.

members.summary: What a MeanFlow training step reports.
examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.mean_flow._model import MeanFlowOutput
>>> out = MeanFlowOutput(
...     loss=lucid.zeros(()),
...     prediction=lucid.zeros(1, 3, 32, 32),
...     target=lucid.zeros(1, 3, 32, 32),
... )
>>> out.prediction.shape, out.target.shape
((1, 3, 32, 32), (1, 3, 32, 32))
The target is returned alongside because it is computed, not given —
it depends on the model's own output at another time, so a caller
cannot reconstruct it afterwards.

attributes.name: loss
attributes.description: The adaptively weighted regression error, a scalar.

attributes.name: prediction
attributes.description:
`(B, C, H, W)` — the model's average velocity
$u_\theta(z_t, r, t)$ at the sampled times.

attributes.name: target
attributes.description:
The stop-gradiented target the prediction is regressed onto.
Reported because the gap between the two *is* the objective, and
because a target that has drifted from the prediction's scale is
the first symptom of a mis-specified tangent.

summary: MeanFlow — one-step generation by modelling the average velocity.
extended:
Geng, Deng, Bai, Kolter and He, [arXiv:2505.13447](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13447), 2025.  The fifth step
of the flow lineage and the one that removes the integral: where Flow
Matching learns the instantaneous velocity and integrates it at sampling
time, MeanFlow learns the average velocity over an interval, which *is*
that integral, and reads a sample off a single evaluation.
citation: Geng, Zhengyang, Mingyang Deng, Xingjian Bai, J. Zico Kolter, and Kaiming He. "Mean Flows for One-step Generative Modeling." arXiv preprint [arXiv:2505.13447](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13447), 2025.
theory:
Flow Matching models the **instantaneous** velocity $v(z_t, t)$
— the tangent of the path at one instant — and recovers a sample by
integrating it.  MeanFlow models the **average** velocity over an
interval, defined as that integral divided by its width:



$$
u(z_t, r, t) \triangleq \frac{1}{t - r}\int_r^t v(z_\tau, \tau)\,d\tau .
$$

The two coincide only in the limit $r \to t$.  Away from it the
average velocity points along the *displacement* between the two
times rather than along the curve, which is exactly what a one-step
sampler needs: with $u$ in hand the whole path is
$z_r = z_t - (t - r)\,u(z_t, r, t)$, and generation from noise
is a single evaluation at $(r, t) = (0, 1)$.

Training on that definition directly would require the integral.  The
way through is to multiply it out and differentiate with respect to
$t$, holding $r$ fixed, which turns the integral into the
**MeanFlow Identity**:



$$
u(z_t, r, t) = v(z_t, t) - (t - r)\,\frac{d}{dt}u(z_t, r, t).
$$

Every term on the right is available.  The instantaneous velocity is
the closed-form conditional velocity Flow Matching already regresses
onto, and the total derivative expands by the chain rule into



$$
\frac{d}{dt}u(z_t, r, t) = v(z_t, t)\,\partial_z u + \partial_t u,
$$

which is one Jacobian-vector product of $u_\theta$ along the
tangent $(v,\, 0,\, 1)$ — a single extra forward-mode pass, not
a second-order solve.  The identity becomes a regression target,



$$
u_{\mathrm{tgt}} = v_t - (t - r)\bigl(v_t\,\partial_z u_\theta
                                    + \partial_t u_\theta\bigr),
$$

and the loss is $\lVert u_\theta - \mathrm{sg}(u_{\mathrm{tgt}}) \rVert^2$.  The stop-gradient is what keeps the cost at one extra
pass: without it the Jacobian-vector product would itself need to be
differentiated.

Setting $r = t$ collapses the second term and recovers Flow
Matching exactly, so the method is Flow Matching with a modified
target rather than a different framework.  The paper draws
$r \neq t$ for only a quarter of samples; at 0% it *is* Flow
Matching and one-step generation fails outright (FID 328.91 against
61.06).
